judgment_text:
In the Supreme Court of Bangladesh 
High Court Division 
(Civil Revisional Jurisdiction) 
Present: 
Mr. Justice Md. Riaz Uddin Khan 
 
Civil Revision No. 1739 of 2012  
  
IN THE MATTER OF : 
An application under section 115(1) of the Code of 
Civil Procedure 
-And- 
In the Matter of: 
Omar Kader Chowdhury 
       ... Petitioner 
 
 
Versus 
Principal Rafiqul Islam and others 
... Opposite parties 
Mr. Abdul Momen Chowdhury, Advocate 
                               ... For the petitioner 
 
 
 
Mr. Kamal-ul-Alam, Advocate with 
Ms. Shahanaj Akther, Advocate 
 
 
 
 
 
 
... For the Opposite Party No. 14 
 
Judgment on: 14.07.2026 
 
Md. Riaz Uddin Khan, J: 
 
 
This civil revision was filed in delay of 540 
days which was condoned provisionally subject to any 
lawful objection to be raised at the time of hearing. 
The Rule was issued asking the opposite parties to show 
cause as to why the Order No. 107 dated 28.02.2010 
passed by the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Sadar, 
Chittagong in Miscellaneous Case No. 41 of 2005 making 
the award dated 16.01.1997 rule of the Court should not 
be set aside and or such other or further order or 
orders should not be passed as to this Court may deem 
fit and appropriate.  
Succinct facts for disposal of this Rule are 
that one Halimun Nessa Chowdhurany along with her 3 
(three) sons and one daughter (opposite parties 12-16 


 
2
herein) filed Other Suit No. 168 of 1993 against the 
defendants (opposite parties 16-30 herein) including 
the 
present 
petitioner 
of 
this 
civil 
revision 
(defendant No.9) before the Court of Assistant Judge, 
Banshkhali (Satkania Chouki), Chattogram praying for 
declaration of title of the land of schedule No.2 of 
the plaint and for further declaration that the 
defendant Nos. 1-9 had got no title therein.  
At one stage of the suit the plaintiff No.1 and 
defendant No.1 filed an application before the court 
praying for allowing them 03 months time for settling 
the dispute through arbitration by arbitrators as 
mentioned in the margin of the application. The learned 
Assistant Judge, Banshkhali, Satkania, Chattogram by 
his order No.13 dated 30.11.1996 allowed 02 (two) 
months time for taking steps.  
Thereafter, 
the 
parties 
made 
arbitration 
agreements dated 07.11.1996 and 27.11.1996 for settling 
their dispute in respect of 99.49 decimals of land 
mentioned in the schedule of the plaint. Thereafter, 
the arbitrators make an award on 16.01.1997. Then on 
27.02.1997 the plaintiffs of that suit filed an 
application 
in 
the 
Court 
of 
Assistant 
Judge, 
Banshkhali, Satkania, Chattogram (where the suit was 
pending) for making the arbitration award dated 
16.01.1997 a rule of the Court by way of amendment of 
the pleadings against which the defendant No. 1 therein 
filed an objection and after hearing, the Assistant 
Judge by his order No.24 dated 15.06.1997 rejected that 
application against which the plaintiffs filed civil 
revision No. 3039 of 1997 before the High Court 
Division and the High Court Division initially issued 


 
3
Rule and stayed the proceedings of the Other Suit No. 
168 of 1993 and ultimately after hearing both the 
parties, the Rule was discharged vide judgment and 
order dated 25.06.2001 affirming the order passed by 
the trial court.  
In the meantime, on 15.04.1997 on the request 
of plaintiff No.4, Aminur Rashid Chowdhury (the present 
opposite party No.14), the Arbitrators filed an 
application under section 14(2) read with section 17 of 
the Arbitration Act, 1940 (hereinafter referred to as 
the Act) before the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, 
Chattogram for making the award dated 16.01.1997 a rule 
of the Court. Initially it was registered as other suit 
No.15 of 1997 and subsequently when the mistake was 
detected it was registered as Miscellaneous Case No.41 
of 2005. In this Miscellaneous Case the opposite 
parties 1-5 and 6-21 appeared and filed two sets of 
separate written objections. However, after hearing, 
the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Chattogram long 
after 13 years allowed this application and was pleased 
to make the award dated 16.01.1997 a rule of the Court 
by his judgment and order dated 28.02.2010.  
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the 
said judgment and order dated 28.02.2010 the present 
petitioner filed the instant civil revision under 
section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure before 
this Court and obtained the Rule as stated at the very 
outset.  
Mr. Abdul Momen Chowdhury, the learned Advocate 
appearing for the petitioner submits that the Joint 
District Judge exceeded his jurisdiction in making the 
award a rule of the Court as there was no agreement for 


 
4
resolving the dispute through arbitration as earlier in 
Other Suit No. 168 of 1993 pending before the court of 
Senior Assistant Judge, Banshkhali, Chattogram by order 
No.24 dated 15.06.1997 rejected the similar application 
filed by the plaintiffs. Earlier on the application of 
the plaintiffs the learned Assistant Judge vide order 
dated 15.06.1997 categorically stated that the court 
did not give any permission to the parties or referred 
for arbitration and as per section 21 to 23 of the 
Arbitration Act, 1940 there cannot be any arbitration 
and hence the trial court rejected the same and the 
arbitrators have come before a different court having 
no jurisdiction for making the award a rule of the 
Court which is not sustainable in law and liable to be 
set aside. Since the dispute was pending in a suit 
namely Other Class Suit No. 168 of 1993 without the 
permission of that court there was no scope for 
Arbitration and the so-called arbitration having no 
basis in accordance with law, the Joint District Judge 
committed error of law in getting the so-called award 
and making the same a rule of the Court.  
The learned advocate next submits that the 
arbitrators cannot substitute their own assessment of 
pecuniary value in complete disregard of the value 
already determined by parties in the suit before the 
Assistant Judge, Banshkhali as Tk-50,000/- and as such 
enhancing and re-fixing a new valuation of Tk-120,000/- 
by the Arbitrators is arbitrary and illegal, on the 
basis of which the arbitration award is liable to be 
set aside. The award should have been filed in the 
court of Assistant Judge, Banshkhali, Chottogram, where 
the Other Suit No. 168 of 1993 was pending between the 


 
5
contending parties including the subject matter of the 
award without enhancing and refixing the valuation.    
Mr. Chowdhury finally submits that the impugned 
judgment and order of the learned Joint District Judge 
was passed in the misconception of law and facts 
resulting in total failure of justice.  
Per contra, Mr. Kamal-Ul-Alam along with Ms. 
Shahanaj Akther, the learned advocate appearing for the 
opposite party No.14 submits that admittedly this civil 
revision has been filed in delay of 540 days without 
any explanation, not to speak of each and every day 
delays as such the instant civil revision is liable to 
be discharged on that ground only. Only a statement has 
been made that the petitioner’s advocate did not inform 
about the impugned judgment in time causing 540 days 
delay. Such delay cannot be condoned because the fact 
remains the petitioner appeared and filed written 
objection in the said miscellaneous case and was 
getting/keeping information as to proceedings and 
result of said miscellaneous case. The Code of Civil 
Procedure deals with procedural laws grounded on 
principle of natural justice and equity will not come 
in aid of indolent party who is not vigilant like the 
petitioner. On this point he referred the cases 
reported in 35 DLR (AD) 51, 1994 BLD (AD) 234 and 1997 
BLD (AD) 57.  
The learned advocate then submits that the 
application dated 15.04.1997 under section 14(2) and 17 
of the Act before the Joint District Judge in Misc. 
Case no. 41/2005 is maintainable. Because, on the 
application dated 30.11.1996 of the parties the 
Assistant Judge, Banshkhali allowed 2 months time to 


 
6
the parties to settle their dispute in the suit in 
Other Class Suit No. 168/1993 out of court through 
Arbitration. It is therefore apparent that although the 
matter in dispute between the parties was pending 
before Court of Assistant Judge, it could be presumed 
that the said Court impliedly treated the said 
application dated 30.11.1996 for time as application 
U/S 14(2) and 17 of the Act for referring the matter to 
Arbitrators. The Arbitrators in their application dated 
15.04.1997 of Misc. Case No. 41/2005 duly made 
statement about the said permission granting 2 months 
time to the parties to settle their dispute in respect 
of the matter in Other Class suit no.168/1993 through 
Arbitration. The Arbitrators assuming that the parties 
were duly accorded permission by the Court to settle 
the dispute in suit out of court through Arbitration 
and duly arbitrated the matter and passed the Award. 
Since the Award was given in relation to the disputed 
immovable properties measuring 99.49 decimals the same 
was valued by the parties for registration at Tk. 
1,20,000/-. Since the Award in respect of the land was 
valued Tk.1,20,000/- the Arbitrators at the request of 
one of the parties Aminur Rashid filed the application 
under sections 14(2) and 17 of the Arbitration Act 
before the appropriate court of the Joint District 
Judge having pecuniary jurisdiction of Tk. 1,20,000/- 
as the same could not have been filed before the Court 
of Assistant Judge as it had pecuniary jurisdiction 
only up to Tk. 50,000/-.  
The learned advocate next submits that the 
petitioner Omar Kader has neither filed any objection 
nor contested in the Misc. Case no. 41/2005 and as such 


 
7
the Court of the Joint District Judge is also empowered 
under the proviso of Section 47 to consider the Award 
obtained otherwise than under sections 21-23 as a 
compromise or adjustment of the suit by the court 
having 
pecuniary 
jurisdiction 
entertained 
the 
Arbitrators' application under section 14(2) and passed 
a Judgment thereon making the Award a rule of the Court 
under section 17 on the consent of the Parties. 
However, Opposite Parties 6 to 21 filed the written 
statement but ultimately they did not appear and 
contest the matter at the time of hearing of Misc. Case 
as was found by the Joint District Judge in the 
impugned judgment and order. The petitioner though 
filed Vokalatnama neither filed any W/Obj, W/S nor 
appeared and contested the matter at the time of 
hearing of the said Misc. Case but has filed the 
present Civil Revision. In this Revision the Petitioner 
has not made any statement that there was no Agreement 
for Arbitration between the parties but the Award shows 
Petitioner was opposite party 16 in the Arbitration 
proceedings and all the parties by Agreement dated 
27.11.1996 conferred jurisdiction on the Arbitrators to 
arbitrate.  
Mr. 
Alam 
emphatically 
submits 
that 
the 
submission that there was no order of the Court of 
Assistant Judge in O.C Suit No. 168/1993 referring the 
dispute in the suit to the Arbitrators under sections 
21 & 23 of the Act and as such the disputed Award of 
the Arbitrators without such reference cannot be made 
rule of the Court by the court of the Joint District 
Judge, is not correct on various grounds. Firstly, the 
foundation of an arbitration is the Arbitration 


 
8
Agreement. Section 14(2) provides that on the request 
of any party to the Arbitration Agreement, the 
Arbitrators may file in the Court the Award which may 
pass a decree making the Award a rule of the Court 
under section 17 of the Act. Section 17 prescribed that 
Court on such an application under section 14(2), may 
pass a Judgment in terms of the Award upon fulfilling 
the conditions laid down therein. Secondly, the 
Petitioner has filed the present Civil Revision against 
the judgment and order dated 28.02.2010 passed by the 
Joint District Judge in Misc. Case No. 41 of 2005 filed 
by the Arbitrators at the request of a party under 
sections 14(2) & 17 making the Award dated 16.01.1997 a 
rule of the Court and not under section 21, as such the 
question of any reference under section 21 does not 
arise at all. Thirdly, the Petitioner has not filed any 
objection under section 33 against the application in 
Misc. Case no. 41/2005 filed by the Arbitrators on the 
request of one of the party. The petitioner also has 
not filed any appeal under section 17 against the 
impugned Judgment and order passed in Misc. Case no. 
41/2005 filed under section 14(2) and 17 of the Act. 
The petitioner also has not agitated any ground that 
the order making the Award a rule of the Court by the 
Joint District Judge (i) is in excess of, or (ii) not 
otherwise in accordance with Award, the only 02 grounds 
as mandated in section 17 on which the judgment and 
order passed under section 17 making the Award a rule 
of the Court can be challenged. Fourthly, the said 
Misc. Case No. 41/2005 was filed under section 14(2) 
and 17 of the Act by the Arbitrators at the request of 
one of the party to the Arbitration Agreement for 


 
9
pronouncement of a Judgment under section 17 of the Act 
making the Award a rule of the Court and to draw decree 
thereon having pecuniary jurisdiction of the subject 
matter of the arbitration at Tk. 1,20,000/-. And as 
such the question of any reference of the dispute to 
the Arbitrators themselves under section 21 of the Act 
to draw an Award does not arise at all.  
The learned advocate strenuously submits that 
Order dated 15.06.1997 passed by the Assistant Judge in 
O.C Suit no. 168/1993 is without jurisdiction as the 
Judge held that the application for amendment of the 
plaint for making the Award a rule of the Court cannot 
be entertained on the ground that court did not refer 
the dispute to the Arbitrators to arbitrate under 
section 21 & 23(1) of the Act and as such it cannot be 
made a rule of the Court. But the selfsame court found 
& held that the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court is 
Tk.50,000/- but the value of the Award is Tk. 
1,20,000/- which is beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction 
of the court and as such the application for making the 
Award a rule of the Court by way of amendment cannot be 
considered. The Assistant Judge has himself found and 
decided that it has no pecuniary jurisdiction to 
entertain the application for making the Award of the 
Arbitrators a rule of the Court but still it went on 
into the merit of the matter holding that it cannot 
make the Award a rule of the Court as it was made 
without a reference under section 21 & 23 as such the 
said order is without jurisdiction and therefore void. 
The civil revision no. 3039/1997 was also misconceived 
and without jurisdiction which was filed against the 
Order dated 15.06.1997 passed by the Assistant Judge in 


 
10
O.C Suit no. 168/1993 holding that: (i) Plaintiff’s 
application was not filed upon compliance of reference 
to Arbitrators by an order of the Court under sections 
21 to 23 of the Act and (ii) The Court has pecuniary 
jurisdiction of Tk.50,000/- and as such has no 
jurisdiction to entertain an application in respect of 
the disputed matter valued at Tk. 1,20,000/-. In view 
of 
the 
above 
categorical 
finding 
of 
lack 
of 
Jurisdiction the Civil Revision against the Judgment of 
Assistant Judge on the merit of the dispute is 
misconceived. Consequently, the Judgment in the said 
Civil Revision no. 3039/1997 on the merit of the 
dispute by the Trial Court is without jurisdiction & 
misconceived. It is apparent there was no judicial 
adjudication of any application for making the Award 
dated 16.01.1997 a rule of the Court in the said O.C 
Suit no.168/1993 and Civil Revision no. 3039/1997. A 
Court which has got no jurisdiction over a matter shall 
not go into the merit of the case and as such any Order 
or Judgment passed by any such court is void. Failure 
to raise objection as to the jurisdiction of the court 
to try a suit or case cannot confer a jurisdiction to a 
court which lawfully does not have jurisdiction to hear 
the said matter and any decree or order passed by such 
court is without jurisdiction and is a nullity. 
Application dated 15.04.1997 under sections 14(2) and 
17 before the Joint District Judge for making the Award 
a rule of the Court was not a res judicata only because 
of the application filed on 27.02.1997 in O.C Suit 
no.168/1993 for making the Award a rule of the Court by 
way of amendment, as no issue as to merit of the matter 
was decided and as such the subsequent application 


 
11
dated 15.04.1997 cannot be said to be barred by res 
judicata. 
Secondly, 
when 
the 
application 
dated 
27.02.1997 was adjudicated on 15.06.1997 by the 
Assistant Judge the application dated 15.04.1997 was 
already pending before the Joint District Judge in 
Misc. Case no. 41/2005 (15/1997) which was however 
adjudicated long thereafter on 28.02.2010 against which 
the present Civil Revision No. 1739 of 2012 is filed 
before this Court. Thirdly, the Assistant Judge having 
admittedly no pecuniary jurisdiction the adjudication 
on merit of the legality of the Award without reference 
under section 21 of the Act is without jurisdiction and 
as such no question of Res judicata arises. 
The learned advocate for the opposite party 
No.14 also submits that admittedly the arbitration was 
not held with the permission of the court but the 
arbitration was held otherwise as per section 47 of the 
Act, the arbitration was rightly held and the court 
accepting that award and making it a rule of the court 
under section 17 of the Arbitration Act did not commit 
any mistake hence the rule is liable to be discharged.  
The learned advocate further submits that an 
application under section 30 of the Act can be filed in 
Court for setting aside the Award on any of the grounds 
mentioned therein. But in the present case no such 
application has been filed by the petitioner. Section 
33 provides that any party to the Arbitration Agreement 
by filing application may challenge the existence or 
validity of the Agreement or an Award. And the Court 
can decide such question on Affidavit. But the proviso 
provides that no such application challenging the 
existence or validity of the Arbitration Agreement or 


 
12
Award shall be entertained by the Court, unless the 
applicant furnishes security for fulfillment of any 
obligation by him under the Award. The Petitioner or 
any opposite parties of that Misc case did not file 
Application under section 33 in the Court of Joint 
District Judge. The petitioner also has not filed any 
Written Objection against the Plaintiff's application 
though some opposite parties have filed Written 
Statement and this may however be treated to be an 
objection under section 33 but since no security has 
been furnished by the same cannot be treated and 
adjudicated under section 33 which was also barred by 
Limitation. Any person who is a non-party to the 
Arbitration Agreement, denying the existence of any 
Agreement can bring a suit under section 33 of the Act 
for declaration that he is not a party to the 
Arbitration Agreement. The Petitioner having not filed 
any objection under section 33 his remedy lies in 
filing a suit under section 33 of the Act before 
appropriate court. 
Mr. Alam finally submits that the present civil 
revision is not maintainable as the impugned judgment 
and order dated 28.02.2010 passed by the Joint District 
Judge, 3rd Court, Chattogram in Miscellaneous Case No. 
41 of 2005 making the award dated 16.01.1997 a rule of 
the Court under section 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 
against which an appeal lies under the provision of 
section 39(1) (i) and (vi) read with section 17 of the 
Act. However, Mr. Alam admits that this Court can 
convert the civil revision petition into Memorandum of 
appeal, if the Court thinks it fit and appropriate.  


 
13
I have heard the submissions advanced at the 
bar, perused the application, supplementary affidavit, 
counter affidavit, reply of the counter affidavit along 
with the annexures. I have also gone through the Lower 
Court Record of Miscellaneous Case No. 41 of 2005. I 
have carefully examined the impugned judgment and 
order.  
In this case both the learned advocates raised 
many questions before this Court referring many 
sections of the Arbitration Act, 1940 with citation of 
series of reported cases but the main contention of the 
petitioner is that since there was a suit pending 
before the Assistant Judge, Banshkhali, Chattogram and 
during pendency of that suit the plaintiff No.1 and 
defendant No.1 filed an application before that court 
seeking time to take steps for arbitration and time was 
allowed for taking steps and thereafter they hold the 
arbitration without permission of the court which is 
not permissible under law. According to the learned 
advocate of the petitioner the arbitration is to be 
dealt with as per Chapter-IV (sections 21 to 25) of the 
Arbitration Act, 1940 when a suit is pending before any 
court.  
On the other hand, the contention of the 
learned advocate for the opposite party No.14 is that 
the Arbitration Act, 1940 permits the parties for 
arbitration otherwise by obtaining permission from the 
court and the present civil revision is barred by 
limitation.  
In dealing with this main contention it would 
be 
profitable 
if 
the 
relevant 
sections 
of 
the 
Arbitration Act, 1940 are reproduced. Section 14 of the 


 
14
Act deals with arbitration without intervention of a 
Court which states-  
Section-14. Award to be signed and filed-(1) When 
the arbitrators or umpire have made their award, 
they shall sign it and shall give notice in 
writing to the parties of the making and signing 
thereof and of the amount of fees and charges 
payable in respect of the arbitration and award. 
(2) The arbitrators or umpire shall, at the 
request of any party to the arbitration agreement 
or any person claiming under such party or if so 
directed by the Court and upon payment of the fees 
and charges due in respect of the arbitration and 
award and of the costs and charges of filing the 
award, cause the award or a signed copy of it, 
together with any depositions and documents which 
may have been taken and proved before them, to be 
filed in Court, and the Court shall thereupon give 
notice to the parties of the filing of the award. 
(3) Where the arbitrators or umpire state a 
special case under clause (b) of section 13, the 
Court, after giving notice to the parties and 
hearing them, shall pronounce its opinion thereon 
and such opinion shall be added to, and shall form 
part of, the award. 
Section 17 also fall under the chapter which deals 
with the arbitration without intervention of a 
Court reads as under- 
Section-17. Judgment in terms of award- Where the 
Court sees no cause to remit the award or any of 
the 
matters 
referred 
to 
arbitration 
for 
reconsideration or to set aside the award, the 


 
15
Court shall, after the time for making an 
application to set aside the award has expired, or 
such application having been made, after refusing 
it, proceed to pronounce judgment according to the 
award, and upon the judgment so pronounced a 
decree shall follow, and no appeal shall lie from 
such decree except on the ground that it is in 
excess of, or not otherwise in accordance with, 
the award. 
Section 20 under Chapter-III deals with the 
arbitration with intervention of a Court where 
there is no suit pending.  
Section 21 under Chapter-IV deals with arbitration 
in suits which is quoted below-  
Section-21. Parties to suit may apply for order of 
reference- Where in any suit all the parties 
interested agree that any matter in difference 
between them in the suit shall be referred to 
arbitration, they may at any time before judgment 
is pronounced apply in writing to the Court for an 
order of reference. 
Section 22 is also under Chapter-IV which reads as 
under-  
Section-22. 
Appointment 
of 
arbitrator- 
The 
arbitrator shall be appointed in such manner as 
may be agreed upon between the parties. 
Section-23 also under the same chapter reads as 
below- 
Section 23. Order of reference- (1) The Court 
shall, by order, refer to the arbitrator the 
matter in difference which he is required to 
determine, and shall in the order specify such 


 
16
time as it thinks reasonable for the making of the 
award. 
(2) Where matter is referred to arbitration, the 
Court shall not, save in the manner and to the 
extent provided in this Act, deal with such matter 
in the suit. 
Section 
25 
also 
under 
Chapter-IV 
provides- 
Section-25. Provisions applicable to arbitrations 
under this Chapter- The provisions of the other 
Chapters shall, so far as they can be made 
applicable, apply to arbitrations under this 
Chapter: 
Provided that the Court may, in any of the circum-
stances mentioned in sections 8, 10, 11 and 12 
instead of filling up the vacancies or making the 
appointments, 
make 
an 
order 
superseding 
the 
arbitration and proceed with the suit, and where 
the 
Court 
makes 
an 
order 
superseding 
the 
arbitration under section 19, it shall proceed 
with the suit. 
Section 30 under Chapter-V deals with grounds for 
setting aside award is quoted below- 
Section 30. Grounds for setting aside award- An 
award shall not be set aside except on one or more 
of the following grounds, namely:-  
(a) that an arbitrator or umpire has misconducted 
himself or the proceedings;  
(b) that an award has been made after the issue of 
an order by the Court suspending the arbitration 
or after arbitration proceedings have become 
invalid under section 35;  


 
17
(c) that an award has been improperly procured or 
is otherwise invalid.  
Section-31 under same chapter deals with the 
jurisdiction of the Court is as follows- 
Section 31. Jurisdiction- (1) Subject to the 
provisions of this Act, an award may be filed in 
any Court having jurisdiction in the matter to 
which the reference relates. 
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in any 
other law for the time being in force and save as 
other-wise provided in this Act, all questions 
regarding the validity, effect or existence of an 
award or an arbitration agreement between the 
parties to the agreement or persons claiming under 
them shall be decided by the Court in which the 
award under the agreement has been, or may be, 
filed and by no other Court. 
(3) All applications regarding the conduct of 
arbitration proceedings or otherwise arising out 
of such proceedings shall be made to the Court 
where the award has been, or may be, filed and by 
no other Court. 
(4) Notwithstanding anything contained elsewhere 
in this Act or in any other law for the time being 
in force, where in any reference any application 
under this Act has been made in a Court competent 
to entertain it, that Court alone shall have 
jurisdiction over the arbitration proceedings and 
all subsequent applications arising out of that 
reference and the arbitration proceedings shall be 
made in that Court and in no other Court. 


 
18
Section-33. Arbitration agreement or award to be 
contested 
by 
application- 
Any 
party 
to 
an 
arbitration agreement or any person claiming under 
him desiring to challenge the existence or 
validity of an arbitration agreement or an award 
or to have the effect of either determined shall 
apply to the Court and the Court shall decide the 
question on affidavits; 
Provided that where the Court deems it just and 
expedient, it may set down the application for 
hearing on other evidence also, and it may pass 
such orders for discovery and particulars as it 
may do in a suit; 
Provided that no application challenging the 
existence or validity of an award or for having 
its effect determined shall be entertained by the 
Court unless the applicant has deposited in the 
Court the amount which he is required to pay under 
the award or has furnished security to the 
satisfaction of the Court for the payment of such 
sum or for the fulfilment of any other obligation 
by him under the award. 
Section-39 under Chapter-VI deals with appeals 
which is quoted below- 
Section 39. Appealable orders- (1) An appeal shall 
lie from the following orders passed under this 
Act (and from no others) to the Court authorised 
by law to hear appeals from original decrees of 
the Court passing the order: 
An order- 
(i) superseding an arbitration;  


 
19
(ii) on an award stated in the form of a special 
case;  
(iii) 
modifying or correcting an award;  
(iv) filing or refusing to file an arbitration 
agreement;  
(v) staying or refusing to stay legal proceedings 
where there is an arbitration agreement;  
(vi) setting aside or refusing to set aside an 
award: 
Provided that the provisions of this section shall 
not apply to any order passed by a Small Cause 
Court. 
(2) No second appeal shall lie from an order 
passed in appeal under this section, but nothing 
in this section shall affect or take away any 
right to appeal to the Supreme Court. 
Section-47 under Chapter-VII (Miscellaneous) is 
quoted below- 
Section 47. Act to apply to all arbitration-
Subject to the provisions of section 46, and save 
insofar as is otherwise provided by any law for 
the time being in force, the provisions of this 
Act shall apply to all arbitrations and to all 
proceedings thereunder: 
Provided that an arbitration award otherwise 
obtained may with the consent of all the parties 
interested be taken into consideration as a 
compromise or adjustment of a suit by any Court 
before which the suit is pending. 
Now, the main controversy between the parties 
in the instant civil revision is that whether the award 
can be made a rule of the court, as has been made in 


 
20
the instant case by the Joint District judge while a 
suit was pending before the court of Assistant judge on 
the same subject matter amongst the same parties. 
Admittedly, there was a suit being Other Class Suit No. 
168 of 1993 pending before the court of Assistant 
Judge, Banshkhali, Chattogram and it is also admitted 
that an application was filed mentioning that the 
parties are willing to mitigate their dispute through 
arbitration further mentioning the names of the 7 
(seven) arbitrators in the margin of the application 
and ultimately sought two months time and the court 
allowed two months time for taking steps. It is also 
admitted that the trial court did not give permission 
to the parties or did not make reference to the 
arbitrator(s) the matter to be resolved through 
arbitration. The learned advocate for the opposite 
party no.14 by his eloquent submissions tried to 
impress this Court that though there was a suit pending 
before the court but the arbitration held without 
permission of the court hence it will come under 
section 47 of the Arbitration Act, 1940 and the Joint 
District Judge did not commit any wrong in making the 
award a rule of the Court. Section 47 of the Act has 
already been quoted above. From plain reading of the 
section it appears that it makes all the provisions of 
the Act applicable to all arbitrations and to all 
proceedings thereunder subject to some condition.  It 
further provides that an arbitration award, otherwise 
obtained, may with the consent of all the parties 
interested be taken into consideration as a compromise 
or adjustment of a suit by any Court before which the 
suit is pending.  


 
21
In the Arbitration Act, 1940 the legislature 
deals with different types of arbitration. Chapter-II 
(sections 3 to 19) deals with arbitration without 
intervention of a Court. Chapter-III (section 20) deals 
the arbitration with intervention of a court where 
there is no suit pending and Chapter-IV (sections 21 to 
25) deals with arbitration in suits pending before 
court. Since admittedly, there was a suit pending 
before the Assistant Judge, Banshkhali, Chattogram and 
the plaintiff No.1 and defendant No.1 filed a joint 
application before that court for an arbitration but 
sought only time which was allowed by the court, it 
cannot be said that the Arbitrators were permitted or 
any reference was made to them by the court for 
arbitration. When there is a suit pending before any 
court the Act provides for arbitration to follow the 
provisions under Chapter-IV (sections 21 to 25) of the 
Act. In that case the parties can file an application 
under section 21 of the Act for arbitration and the 
court under section 22 may appoint arbitrator(s) by the 
court itself or as prayed by the parties and under 
section 23 the court finally refers the matter to the 
arbitrator(s) but in the present case there was no such 
reference made by the court to the arbitrators which 
was also conceded by the learned advocate of the 
opposite party. From the above facts it is clear that 
with a misconception of the facts and law the 
arbitrators thought they were empowered by the order of 
the court for arbitration but the record reveals that 
the arbitrators were not permitted or referred for 
arbitration 
by 
the 
court. 
In 
the 
facts 
and 
circumstances of the case as stated above, I am of the 


 
22
view, that the learned Joint District Judge committed 
error of law in entertaining such an award making it a 
rule 
of 
the 
court 
when 
parties 
earlier 
sought 
permission from the court of Assistant Judge where a 
suit was pending. 
From plain reading of section 39 of Arbitration 
Act it appears that any order passed by the court 
superseding an Arbitration on an award stated in the 
form of special case modifying or correcting an award 
for filing or refusing to stay legal proceedings where 
there is an Arbitration agreement, appeal can be filed 
on 6 grounds against the order for setting aside or 
refusing to set aside the agreement and award. In the 
present case the impugned judgment and order passed 
under section 17 of the Act, which is in fact a decree, 
cannot be said passed which can be challenged in appeal 
in any of these 6 grounds. From section 17 of the Act 
it appears that any judgment passed under this section 
will be treated as decree of the court and no appeal 
shall lie against this decree except on two grounds, 
that is, on the ground that it is in excess of, or not 
otherwise in accordance with, the award. In the present 
case the impugned judgment is passed under section 17 
of the Arbitration Act. Hence it is, as per section 17, 
a decree. This civil revision has been filed admittedly 
not challenging on the ground that it is excess of or 
not otherwise in accordance with the award. Hence the 
appeal under section 17 also does not lie in the 
present case. We have already noticed that the 
Arbitration 
was 
held 
without 
the 
permission 
or 
reference of the court during pendency of a suit. Hence 
this award is no award in the eye of law and in that 


 
23
sense, in my humble opinion, the appeal does not lie 
and the petitioner’s remedy lies in civil revision. 
This view is supported by a series of decisions 
reported in AIR 1951 Madraj 665, AIR 1952 Calcutta 10, 
AIR 1949 Madraj 256, AIR 1949 Madraj 273. However, Mr. 
Kamal-ul-Alam frankly conceded that if this Court found 
that the appeal lies then a civil revision may be 
converted into appeal and the appeal may also be 
converted into civil revision as well by this Court. In 
that view, on this point no more elaborate discussion 
is necessary.  
The next point regarding the bar of present 
civil revision on limitation, it appears from record, 
that the delay of 540 days in filing the instant civil 
revision were provisionally condoned by this Court. 
Series of decisions have been cited before this Court 
regarding the condonation of delay under section 5 of 
the limitation Act. 
 
In condoning delay under section 5 of the 
limitation Act the Indian Supreme Court, AIR 1987 SC 
1353, adopted a liberal approach condoning the delay 
which was approved by our court in 59 DLR (AD) 1 
wherein it has been stated that- 1. Ordinarily a 
litigant does not stand to benefit by lodging an appeal 
late, 2. Refusing to condone delay can result in a 
meritorious matter being thrown out at the very 
threshold and cause of justice being defeated. As 
against this when delay is condoned the highest that 
can happen is that a cause would be decided on merits 
after hearing the parties, 3. “Every day’s delay must 
be explained” does not mean that a pedantic approach 
should be made. Why not every hour’s delay, every 


 
24
second’s delay? The doctrine must be applied in a 
rational common sense pragmatic manner, 4. When 
substantial justice and technical considerations are 
pitted against each other, cause of substantial justice 
deserves to be preferred for the other side cannot 
claim to have vested right in injustice being done 
because of a non-deliberate delay, 5. There is no 
presumption that delay is occasioned deliberately, or 
on account of mala-fides. A litigant does not stand to 
benefit by recording delay. In fact, he runs a serious 
risk, 6. It must be grasped that judiciary is respected 
not on account of its power to legalise injustice on 
technical grounds but because it is capable of removing 
injustice and is expected to do so. 
I respectfully agree with the above principle 
in dealing with condoning delay and fully endorse it.  
In the light of above principle should this Court 
condone the delay occurred in the instant case which 
was earlier provisionally condoned by this Court? In 
the present case the petitioner explained the delay 
though a bit causal manner stating that the learned 
advocate did not communicate the result of the 
miscellaneous case and after knowing from the opposite 
party when they tried to mutate the land, the 
petitioner came before the court and obtained the 
certificate copy and filed this civil revision. I have 
examined all the order sheets of Miscellaneous Case 
No.41 of 2005 (previously Other Suit No. 15 of 1997) 
from date of filing in 1997 to the date of passing the 
impugned judgment and order in 2010 and it appears from 
the order sheets that the petitioner along with 
opposite parties 6 to 21 (who was opposite party no.21) 


 
25
was present by filing joint written statement all 
through up to 2009. So, it cannot be said that the 
petitioner was indolent or negligent in pursuing his 
cause as the record shows that the petitioner along 
with other opposite parties of the misc case was 
pursuing his cause for more than 10 years and the 
petitioner may have lost communication with the learned 
advocate and I find substance in the submission of the 
learned advocate of the petitioner that there was a 
communication gap between the petitioner and the 
learned 
advocate. 
When 
substantial 
justice 
and 
technical considerations are pitted against each other, 
cause of substantial justice deserves to be preferred 
for the other side cannot claim to have vested right in 
injustice being done because of a non-deliberate delay. 
Hence taking a liberal approach as enunciated by the 
Indian Supreme Court, approved by our Supreme Court, I 
am of the view, the delay was justly condoned by this 
Court at the time of the issuance of the Rule. 
On the submission of the learned advocate for 
the opposite party that the order dated 15.06.1997 
passed by the Assistant judge is a nullity having no 
pecuniary jurisdiction and consequently the judgment 
and order dated 25.06.2001 passed by the High Court 
Division in Civil Revision No.3039 of 1997 is also a 
nullity is not necessary to be determined in disposing 
the instant civil revision. Because on that issue the 
result of this civil revision will not be affected in 
any way. Be that as it may, suffice is to say, that the 
jurisdiction of the court is a root and fundamental 
question 
and 
it 
is 
long 
settled 
that 
any 
order/judgment/decision 
passed 
by 
any 
Court 
or 


 
26
authority 
having 
no 
jurisdiction 
is 
no 
order/judgment/decision in the eye of law. I have 
already opined that the arbitration award dated 
16.01.1997 is no award in the eye of law as it was made 
by the arbitrators without referred by the court of 
Assistant Judge where a suit namely Other Class Suit 
No.168 of 1993 was pending. It cannot be even treated 
as compromise between the agreeing parties under 
section 47 of the Arbitration Act as it is not filed 
before the Court where the suit was pending rather 
filed before the court of Joint district judge 
enhancing the pecuniary valuation of the subject 
matter. When a suit is pending specifically mentioning 
the valuation of the suit, the arbitrators did not have 
any authority to enhance or refix the valuation 
changing the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court.        
In the facts and circumstances and the points 
of law as discussed above the instant civil revision 
merits consideration and I found substance in the 
instant Rule for which I am inclined to interfere with 
the impugned judgment and order dated 28.02.2010, which 
in fact a decree, passed by the Joint District Judge 
making the award, a rule of the Court which is no award 
in the eye of law.  
In the result the Rule is made absolute. 
However, without any order as to cost. 
The judgment and order, (in fact decree) dated 
28.02.2010 passed by the Joint District Judge, 3rd 
Court, Chattogram in Miscellaneous Case No.41 of 2005 
making the award dated 16.01.1997, a rule of the court 
is hereby set aside.  


 
27
This Court is informed that the suit is still 
pending before the trial court. In that view, the trial 
court is directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously 
as early as possible without affording unnecessary 
adjournments keeping in mind that the original suit is 
of the year 1993.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Ziaul Karim 
Bench Officer

judgment_text:
1 
 
Present: 
     Mr. Justice Md. Khasruzzaman 
  
  
 
              Criminal Appeal No. 6402 of 2019 
Khandaker Md. Omor Faruk Kamal  
…………Convict-appellant  
-Versus-  
The State and another  
…………..Respondent  
Mr. Gopal Chanda, Advocate, with 
Mr. Mohammad Iqbal Hossain, Advocate  
……………For convict-appellant  
Mr. Mohammad Abdul Karim, D.A.G. with  
Mr. Md. Azgarul Islam, A.A.G. and  
Ms. Mahfuza Akhter, A.A.G.              
                                       .....For the State. 
Mr. Md. Motahar Hossain (Sazu), Advocate  
……..For the complainant-respondent No. 2.  
Judgment on 13.03.2025 
01. The convict appellant, Khandaker Md. Omor Faruk 
Kamal, has preferred the above numbered appeal against the 
judgment and order of conviction and sentence dated 
29.11.2017 passed by the learned Special Judge, Special 
Judge Court No. 6, Dhaka in Special Sessions Case No. 07 of 
2017, arising out of C.R Case No. 240 of 2017, convicting 
the appellant under section 138 of the Negotiable 
Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him there under to 


2 
 
suffer simple imprisonment for 01(one) year and also to pay 
a fine of Taka 30,00,000.00 (Thirty Lac).  
02. The prosecution case, in short, is that one M.S.I. 
Azad, proprietor of Adib Chemical Company, as a 
complainant filed a petition of complaint under section 138 
of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 in the Court of 
Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka alleging inter alia that 
the complaint is a businessman and the accused is the owner 
of Sadi International. When the complainant asked the 
accused for the money he was owed, the accused drew a 
cheque bearing No. C.A. 100
F  8041752 dated 05.01.2017 in 
account No. 1762901011604 maintained by him with Pubali 
Bank Ltd., Peelkhana Branch, Dhaka amounting to Tk. 
30,00,000.00 (Thirty Lac) to the complainant. The 
complainant presented the cheque in his account of Standard 
Bank Limited, New Eskaton Branch, Dhaka for encashment 
on 11.01.2017 and it was sent to the Pubali Bank Ltd., 
Peelkhana Branch, for collection but it was dishonoured and 
returned to the complainant with the remark insufficient fund 


3 
 
on 11.01.2017. The complainant informed the matter to the 
accused but he did not response. Thereafter, on 15.01.2017 
the complainant sent a legal notice through his learned 
Advocate to the accused by registered post with 
acknowledgement 
due 
requesting 
him 
for 
making 
arrangement of the money so that the cheque can be 
honoured and the accused received the legal notice but he did 
not pay the same. Thus, on 20.02.2017 the complainant 
under the compelling circumstances filed the petition of 
complaint against the accused under section 138 of the 
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 in the Court of Chief 
Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka. 
03. On the basis of the said petition of complaint filed 
by the complainant, the case was registered as C.R Case No. 
240 of 2017. The learned Magistrate examined the 
complainant under section 200 of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure and issued process against the accused. Pursuant 
to the process, on 21.03.2017 the accused appeared before 
the Court of Magistrate and sought bail and accordingly, he 
was granted bail on the same day. Thereafter, the case was 


4 
 
transmitted to the Court of Metropolitan Sessions Judge, 
Dhaka for trial and it was registered as Metro Sessions Case 
No. 7410 of 2017. The Metropolitan Sessions Judge, Dhaka 
took cognizance of the offence under section 138 of the 
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 against the accused and 
thereafter, the case record was transferred to the learned 
Special Judge, Special Judge Court No. 6, Dhaka for trial 
and disposal where the case was again registered and re-
numbered as Special Sessions Case No. 07 of 2017.  
04. On 22.06.2017 the charge was framed under 
section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 against 
the accused in his presence and it was read over and 
explained to the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and 
claimed to be tried. 
05. In order to substantiate the charge against the 
accused, the prosecution examined 01 (one) witness and on 
completion of the recording of evidence from the side of the 
prosecution, the accused was examined under section 342 of 
the Code of Criminal Procedure when he repeated his 


5 
 
innocence and expressed his desire for examination of the 
defence witnesses and accordingly, the defence examined 01 
(one) witness in this case. On 25.09.2017 two defence 
witnesses filed Hazira but the Court was busy in Special 
Case No. 13 of 2017 and as such, these two defence 
witnesses were not examined whereas these two witnesses 
were examined in Special Sessions Case No. 06 of 2017. 
06. The defence case, as projected through cross 
examination of PW- 1 and by adducing defence witness, is 
one of innocence and false implication. The further defence 
case is that the accused did not draw the cheque to clear his 
liabilities as claimed by the complainant. One Monir Hossain 
Mithu, cousin of the complainant, and Hanif Miah were very 
much close to the accused, and the accused had some 
monetary problem and he took shelter of said Monir Hossain 
Mithu and Hanif Miah in order to solve his monetary 
problem; and Monir Hossain Mithu and Hanif Miah assured 
the accused that they would manage loan through the 
complainant. Accordingly, Monir Hossain Mithu and Hanif 
Miah along with the accused had gone to the complainant 


6 
 
with an hope that they would manage some bank loan for the 
accused. After some discussions, the accused gave the 
complainant two cheques signed by him along with some 
papers to get a loan from the bank. But for insufficient of 
papers, the complainant could not manage any loan from the 
bank. Then the complainant gave a loan of Tk. 25,00,000.00 
(Twenty Five Lac) to the accused and at the time of 
disbursement of the money, the complainant took Tk. 
1,00,000.00 (One Lac) in cash from the said Tk. 
25,00,000.00 (Twenty Five Lac) and the complainant kept 
two cheques signed by the accused, which had been 
previously given to him for a loan from the bank. When the 
accused asked the complainant to return the two cheques, the 
complainant said that if the complainant returned the Tk. 
25,00,000.00 (Twenty Five Lac) to the complainant within a 
month, the complainant would return the two cheques to the 
accused. But the complainant using the said 02 cheques filed

Special Sessions Case No. 07 of 2017, was filed for 
dishonouring the cheque bearing No. 8041752. Thus, the 
prosecution side totally failed to prove the charge orally and 
documentary. But the Trial Count passed the judgment and 
order of conviction and sentence of the case without taking 
these points into consideration.  


32 
 
37. It appears from the records that P.W.-1 was 
recalled on 17.10.2017. Upon being recalled, he deposed that 

 @A chemical  '9 import  
। 
 @A

 /। He further 
deposed that

' ?  J । 
In the meantime, the accused obtained information 
from government authorities indicating that the complainant 
was not an importer of the said chemical. On the basis of 
such information, the defence put a suggestion to the 
complainant that he was not an importer of the said 
chemical. 
Subsequently, upon an application filed by the 
complainant-respondent under section 428 of the Code of 
Criminal Procedure, the High Court Division recorded the 
additional evidence of P.W.-1 on 12.06.2022. During cross-
examination, P.W.-1 deposed that 	

33

 7N    O    ,  । 
Therefore, it may be concluded that P.W.-1 initially 
categorically deposed that he had imported 250 metric tons 
of Sodium Bentonite from China and had sold 200 metric 
tons thereof to the accused. Subsequently, however, during 
cross-examination, P.W.-1 deposed that he had not imported 
the chemical himself; rather, he had purchased it from a 
company in Chattogram. 
It is now an admitted fact that the complainant did not 
import the chemical. Consequently, the accused was no 
longer required to prove independently whether the 
complainant had imported the chemical, as P.W.-1 himself 
admitted during cross-examination that he had not imported 
it but had purchased it from a company in Chattogram. 
Accordingly, 
although 
the 
complainant 
initially 
categorically stated that he had imported the chemical and 
had sold 200 metric tons of Sodium Bentonite to the accused, 
he subsequently admitted during cross-examination that he 


34 
 
had not imported it. In view of such subsequent admission, it 
may reasonably be concluded that the complainant resorted 
to various devices in an attempt to establish his case but 
ultimately failed, with the result that his testimony lost its 
credibility. 
38. It appears that D.W-1 deposed that he paid the 
complainant Tk. 10,00,000.00 (Ten Lac) through a pay order 
and Tk. 6,50,000.00 (Six Lac and Fifty Thousand) in cash; 
and D.W-3 deposed that the accused paid Tk. 10,00,000.00 
(Ten Lac) through a pay order and Tk. 6,00,000.00 (Six Lac) 
in cash to the complainant, and D.W-3 was not cross 
examined by the prosecution, and as such, the depositions of 
D.W-3 remained unchallenged and intact. C.W-1 proved that 
the complainant received Tk. 10,00,000.00 (Ten Lac) 
through a pay order, exhibit-I. Now it is decided that the 
complainant received Tk. 10,00,000.00 (Ten Lac) from the 
accused through the pay order. But the complainant 
dishonoured the two cheques of Tk. 60,00,000.00 (Sixty Lac) 
and filed both the cases for punishment and recovery of Tk. 
60,00,000.00 (Sixty Lac) from the accused, which was not 


35 
 
correct decision of the complainant under any circumstances 
as section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act deals with 
for committing of an offence and there is a provision for 
punishment with imprisonment, or with fine, or with both. 
Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act will never be 
used to recover partial money or partial cheque amount of 
the dishonoured cheque. A cheque is a bill of exchange and a 
bill of exchange is an instrument. A bill of exchange shall 
contain an order to pay to its holder and this order will not be 
used partially, and if it is used partially then the document 
will not be treated as a bill of exchange. In the present case, 
as claimed by the complainant and the accused, two different 
transactions were involved. The complainant claimed that he 
sold Sodium Bentonite valued at Tk. 60,00,000.00 (Sixty 
Lac) to the accused. On the other hand, the accused claimed 
that he took a loan of Tk. 24,00,000.00 (Twenty Four Lac) 
from the complainant. The complainant as a plaintiff did not 
file the present case for recovery of the money rather he filed 
the case against the accused for committing an offence. In 
the case of two different transactions, the Court should have 


36 
 
either believed the complainant’s case or disbelieved it. 
Therefore, the judgment of the Trial Court to reduce the 
amount by Tk. 10,00,000.00 (Ten Lac) was not a correct 
decision. 
39. Considering all the aspect of the case it shows that 
no offence has been constituted by dishonouring the cheques 
of the appellant punishable under section 138 of the 
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 
40. In view of the forgoing discussions, I find merit in 
the appeal.  
41. In the result, the appeal is allowed. 
42. Thus, the judgment and order of conviction and 
sentence dated 29.11.2017 passed by the learned Special 
Judge, Special Judge Court No. 6, Dhaka in Special Sessions 
Case No. 07 of 2017, arising out of C.R Case No. 240 of 
2017, convicting the appellant under section 138 of the 
Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 and sentencing him there 
under to suffer simple imprisonment for 01(one) year and 
also to pay a fine of Taka 30,00,000.00 (Thirty Lac) is set 
aside. 


37 
 
43. Accordingly, the convict-appellant is acquitted of 
the charge levelled against him, and he is permitted to 
withdraw the amount deposited by him in the Trial Court for 
the purpose of filing the appeal. 
44. The Trial Court is directed to do needful. 
45. Send down the records.  
46. Communicate the judgment.  
                    (Md. Khasruzzaman, J:)
