case_title: Haji Md. Aslam vs Md. Shafiqul Islam
judgment_text: In agreements for sale of immovable property, fixation of a period for completion does not per se make time the essence of the contract. The intention to make time essential must be clear from the terms or conduct of the parties.
ratio_summary:
In contracts for the sale of immovable property, time is presumed not to be of the essence unless there is an express contractual stipulation or surrounding circumstances showing an intention to make time strictly essential.

[Controlling Statutes: The Contract Act, 1872 (55, 73)]

case_title: Md. Mokhlesur Rahman vs Md. Habibur Rahman and others
judgment_text: Section 52A was inserted in 2004 to eliminate fraudulent transfers. A seller who is not recorded in the latest Khatian and has not paid land development tax cannot execute a valid registered conveyance.
ratio_summary:
Under Section 52A of the Registration Act, 1908, the Sub-Registrar is legally mandated to refuse registration of a sale deed unless the seller presents an updated mutation Khatian and proof of land development tax payment in the seller's name.

[Controlling Statutes: The Registration Act, 1908 (52A), The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (54)]

case_title: Mrs. Nasreen Akhter vs Bangladesh and others
judgment_text: The welfare of the minor is of paramount importance in deciding custody. The rules of personal law regarding the age of Hizanat are subordinate to the welfare and moral wellbeing of the minor child.
ratio_summary:
In child custody disputes under Section 17 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, the welfare of the minor is the paramount consideration, which overrides rigid traditional age thresholds of maternal custody (Hizanat).

[Controlling Statutes: The Guardians and Wards Act, 1890 (17, 25)]

case_title: Md. Altaf Hossain vs The State and another
judgment_text: To constitute an offence of cheating under section 420, dishonest intention must exist at the inception of the contract. Where the allegations disclose only a civil liability, criminal proceedings cannot be permitted as a coercive tool.
ratio_summary:
Mere breach of contract does not give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating or criminal breach of trust under Sections 406/420 of Penal Code unless fraudulent intention is shown at the inception of the transaction. Criminal proceedings used as a tool of coercion for civil debt recovery must be quashed under Section 561A CrPC to prevent abuse of the process of the court.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (561A), The Penal Code, 1860 (406, 420)]

case_title: Abdul Jalil and others vs Md. Joynal Abedin and others
judgment_text: By the amendment of 2004, the legislature has made registration of a contract for sale mandatory under section 17A of the Registration Act and section 54A of the Transfer of Property Act. Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act explicitly bars any court from entertaining a suit for specific performance of an unregistered contract for sale.
ratio_summary:
An agreement for sale of immovable property executed after the 2004 amendment must be compulsorily registered. An unregistered contract for sale is completely barred from being specifically enforced in civil court under Section 21A of the Specific Relief Act, 1877.

[Controlling Statutes: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (54, 54A), The Registration Act, 1908 (17A, 49), The Specific Relief Act, 1877 (21A)]

case_title: Md. Mozibur Rahman vs Government of Bangladesh and others
judgment_text: It is well settled that entry in the record-of-rights does not create title. Record-of-rights is prepared for fiscal purposes, namely, collection of land revenue, and it raises only a rebuttable presumption of correctness regarding possession.
ratio_summary:
A Khatian or Record of Rights (Porcha) does not create nor extinguish title to immovable property. It only raises a rebuttable presumption of possession and tenancy for revenue collection purposes under Section 144(4) of the SAT Act.

[Controlling Statutes: The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (144, 144A), The Evidence Act, 1872 (35)]

case_title: Md. Nurul Islam vs S.M. Shahjahan and others
judgment_text: An order of temporary injunction cannot be granted as a matter of course. The court must be satisfied on three indispensable ingredients: prima facie arguable case, balance of convenience and inconvenience, and irreparable injury.
ratio_summary:
To obtain a temporary injunction under Order 39, Rules 1 and 2 of the CPC, the applicant must establish all three conditions cumulatively: (1) a strong prima facie case, (2) irreparable loss and injury that cannot be compensated in money, and (3) balance of convenience in applicant's favour.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order 39, Rule 1, Order 39, Rule 2)]

case_title: Md. Harun-or-Rashid vs Monowara Begum and others
judgment_text: By inserting clause (aa) in section 17(1) of the Registration Act in 2004, the legislature has brought an end to oral Hiba of immovable property. Registration of an instrument of declaration of Hiba is now compulsory.
ratio_summary:
Following the 2004 amendment to Section 17(1) of the Registration Act, 1908, a declaration of Hiba (gift) under Muslim law regarding immovable property must be made through a registered instrument. An unregistered oral Hiba confers no legal title.

[Controlling Statutes: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (123), The Registration Act, 1908 (17(1))]

case_title: Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST) and others vs Bangladesh and others
judgment_text: Section 54 and section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure must be read strictly in conformity with the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 27, 31, 32, 33 and 35 of the Constitution. No person arrested without warrant shall be detained in custody for a period exceeding twenty-four hours without the authority of a Magistrate, and no accused shall be subjected to torture in custody.
ratio_summary:
Lays down mandatory 15-point operational guidelines for arrest without warrant under Section 54 and interrogation/remand under Section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Reaffirms that detention cannot exceed 24 hours without production before a Magistrate under Section 61 CrPC and Article 33 of the Constitution, and strictly prohibits physical or psychological torture during remand under Article 35(5).

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (54, 61, 167), The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 27, Article 31, Article 32, Article 33, Article 35)]

judgment_text: The First Information Report is not an encyclopaedia of the prosecution case. It is only information of a cognizable offence to set the criminal law into motion. Non-mention of minute details does not vitiate the prosecution case.
ratio_summary:
An FIR is not a substantive piece of evidence; it can only be used to corroborate or contradict its maker under the Evidence Act. An FIR is not required to be an encyclopedia of the entire incident.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (154, 161, 162)]

case_title: Md. Shahidul Islam vs Md. Anowar Hossain
judgment_text: For the purpose of deciding an application under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code, only the plaint averments are material. The court cannot look into the written statement or extraneous materials submitted by the defendant.
ratio_summary:
For deciding an application under Order 7 Rule 11 CPC, the court must look strictly and exclusively at the averments in the plaint. The defense set up in the written statement or annexures cannot be considered at that stage.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order 7, Rule 11)]

case_title: Haji Md. Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh and others
judgment_text: The proviso to section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is mandatory. When the plaintiff is out of possession and in a position to claim recovery of possession, a suit for simple declaration of title is hit by the proviso and must be dismissed.
ratio_summary:
Under the proviso to Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877, no court shall make a declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief such as recovery of possession, omits to do so. A suit for bare declaration by a plaintiff out of possession is barred.

[Controlling Statutes: The Specific Relief Act, 1877 (42)]

case_title: Md. Sirajul Islam vs Begum Feroza Sultana
judgment_text: The jurisdiction to decree specific performance is discretionary, and the court is not bound to grant such relief merely because it is lawful to do so. The plaintiff must aver and prove that he was always ready and willing to perform his essential obligations.
ratio_summary:
Specific performance is a discretionary relief under Section 22 of the Specific Relief Act, 1877. The plaintiff must prove readiness and willingness to perform their part of the contract from the date of the contract continuously up to the date of hearing.

[Controlling Statutes: The Specific Relief Act, 1877 (12, 22)]

case_title: Khaleda Akter vs Md. Tariqul Islam
judgment_text: Prompt dower is exigible on demand and limitation runs from the date of refusal. Deferred dower becomes due only on dissolution of the marriage by death or divorce, and the limitation is three years from the date of dissolution.
ratio_summary:
Prompt dower is payable on demand; limitation of 3 years runs from the date of demand and refusal under Article 103 of Limitation Act. Deferred dower becomes payable on dissolution of marriage by death or divorce; limitation runs 3 years from dissolution under Article 104.

[Controlling Statutes: The Family Courts Act, 2023 (4, 5), The Limitation Act, 1908 (Schedule I, Article 103, Schedule I, Article 104)]

case_title: Government of Bangladesh vs Ayesha Khatun
judgment_text: Section 4 of the Ordinance creates a statutory succession in favour of the children of a predeceased child. The succession opens on the death of the propositus and the children step into the shoes of their deceased parent per stirpes.
ratio_summary:
Under Section 4 of the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961, the children of any predeceased son or daughter inherit the exact per stirpes share which their parent would have received if alive at the time of the grandfather's death.

[Controlling Statutes: The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 (4)]

case_title: Abdul Gafur vs Md. Shamsul Haque
judgment_text: By the substituting amendment of section 96 in 2006, the legislature intentionally omitted contiguous land owners and co-sharers by purchase. Only a co-sharer in the holding by inheritance is entitled to maintain an application for pre-emption.
ratio_summary:
Following the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2006 (Act No. 34 of 2006), the right of pre-emption under Section 96 is restricted strictly to a co-sharer by inheritance of the holding. A co-sharer by purchase or contiguous tenant has no right of pre-emption under Section 96.

[Controlling Statutes: The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (96)]

case_title: Eastern Bank Limited vs Md. Shafiuddin and others
judgment_text: Section 12 of the Ain mandates that the financial institution must make earnest efforts to sell the mortgaged security by auction before approaching the court. Compliance with this provision is a statutory prerequisite.
ratio_summary:
The requirement of attempting sale of mortgaged property under Section 12 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 prior to filing a money claim is mandatory. Any deviation renders subsequent recovery proceedings defective.

[Controlling Statutes: The Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (12, 33)]

case_title: Md. Rafiqul Islam vs Government of Bangladesh
judgment_text: Section 115 of the Code is limited to rectifying errors of jurisdiction. It is not an appellate power and the High Court Division cannot interfere with findings of fact unless they are perverse or based on no evidence.
ratio_summary:
Revisional jurisdiction under Section 115 CPC is restricted to jurisdictional errors, illegal exercise, or material irregularity. The High Court Division cannot sit as a court of second appeal to re-appreciate concurrent findings of fact.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (115)]

case_title: Md. Abul Hossain vs Md. Habibur Rahman
judgment_text: The power to amend pleadings is aimed at serving the ends of justice. However, an amendment which changes the fundamental nature and character of the suit or introduces a time-barred claim cannot be allowed.
ratio_summary:
Amendments under Order 6 Rule 17 CPC should be allowed liberally for determining real questions in controversy, provided the amendment does not introduce a completely new inconsistent cause of action or alter the fundamental character of the suit.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order 6, Rule 17)]

case_title: Mrs. Shima Rani Das vs Narayan Chandra Das and others
judgment_text: The 1937 Act confers upon the widow the same interest in the property as her husband had. Though it is a limited interest known as Hindu Women's Estate, she is fully competent to seek partition of the holding.
ratio_summary:
Under Section 3 of the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937, a Hindu widow inherits the same share as her deceased husband in joint family property, holding a limited life estate with the right to claim partition during her lifetime.

[Controlling Statutes: The Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (3(1), 3(2))]

case_title: The State vs Md. Mofazzal Hossain
judgment_text: The power under section 498 of the Code to grant anticipatory bail is of an exceptional character. It must be exercised with caution where the petitioner establishes a prima facie apprehension of arrest based on motivated or frivolous accusations.
ratio_summary:
Anticipatory bail under Section 498 CrPC is an extraordinary prerogative remedy granted only when there is reasonable apprehension of arrest with mala fide intent or where civil disputes are dressed up as criminal offences to cause harassment.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (498)]

case_title: Yaor Mia (Md) and another vs Haji Shah Dhanai Ali and others
judgment_text: Mutation of names in the revenue record is only for the purpose of payment of rent and does not confer any title. Title to immovable property is governed by the substantive law of transfer and valid conveyance.
ratio_summary:
Mutation of a holding in revenue records does not determine title to immovable property. Title passes upon execution and registration of the deed; mutation is an administrative recording of the taxpayer liable for rent.

[Controlling Statutes: The State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (117, 143)]

case_title: Fazlul Haque vs Md. Enamul Haque
judgment_text: Res Judicata is founded on public policy to prevent multiplicity of litigation. The identity of the subject-matter, the parties, the title, and final adjudication by a competent court are sine qua non for applying section 11.
ratio_summary:
To attract Section 11 CPC, the matter directly and substantially in issue in the subsequent suit must have been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, heard and finally decided by a court of competent jurisdiction.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (11)]

case_title: Md. Rashedul Islam vs The State
judgment_text: Indefinite detention of an undertrial prisoner without any fault on his part amounts to pre-trial punishment. Prolonged detention without trial is a legitimate ground for granting bail under section 498 of the Code.
ratio_summary:
Inordinate and unexplained delay in trial resulting in prolonged pre-trial detention violates the constitutional right to speedy trial under Article 35(3) and constitutes a valid and compelling ground for granting bail under Section 498 CrPC.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (497, 498)]

case_title: Abdul Khaleque vs Mrs. Feroza Begum
judgment_text: Under Article 91 of the Limitation Act, time runs from the date when the facts entitling the plaintiff to have the instrument cancelled or set aside become known to him, and not from the date of registration of the fraudulent deed.
ratio_summary:
In a suit for cancellation of a fraudulent deed under Section 39 of the Specific Relief Act, the 3-year limitation period under Article 91 of the Limitation Act begins to run from the date the plaintiff discovers the facts entitling them to have the instrument cancelled.

[Controlling Statutes: The Specific Relief Act, 1877 (39), The Limitation Act, 1908 (Schedule I, Article 91)]

case_title: Haji Md. Shamsul Alam vs Commissioner of Customs and others
judgment_text: The requirement of serving a show-cause notice under Section 180 of the Customs Act is a statutory embodiment of natural justice. Any adjudication order passed in violation thereof is null and void.
ratio_summary:
Section 180 of the Customs Act, 1969 mandates that no order of confiscation or penalty can be made without giving the owner of goods written notice stating the grounds and a reasonable opportunity of making representation.

[Controlling Statutes: The Customs Act, 1969 (179, 180, 196)]

case_title: Ain O Salish Kendra (ASK) vs Government of Bangladesh
judgment_text: Right to life under Article 32 of the Constitution does not mean mere animal existence. It includes the right to live with human dignity and livelihood. Eviction without prior notice and rehabilitation violates constitutional safeguards.
ratio_summary:
The right to life guaranteed under Article 32 includes the right to livelihood. The state cannot arbitrarily evict slum dwellers without reasonable notice and an opportunity for basic relocation or rehabilitation.

[Controlling Statutes: The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 31, Article 32, Article 102)]

case_title: Abdul Quader Mollah vs Chief Prosecutor
judgment_text: An amendment in procedural law is retrospective in operation and applies to pending proceedings unless the legislature has expressed a contrary intention.
ratio_summary:
Amendments touching purely upon procedural rights, such as creating a right of appeal for the prosecution against inadequacy of sentence, operate retrospectively and apply to pending proceedings unless explicitly barred by statute.

[Controlling Statutes: The International Crimes (Tribunals) Act, 1973 (21), The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 47, Article 47A)]

case_title: Md. Rafiqul Islam vs Government of Bangladesh and others
judgment_text: Mandamus is an extraordinary constitutional remedy to enforce a public legal duty. Where a statutory authority fails or refuses to perform its statutory obligations, the High Court Division under Article 102 has jurisdiction to compel compliance.
ratio_summary:
A Writ of Mandamus will lie to compel a public authority to perform a mandatory duty imposed by statute, provided the petitioner has a legal right to performance and has made a prior demand for justice which was refused or ignored.

[Controlling Statutes: The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 102)]

case_title: Mahbuba Huq vs Dr. Syed Moinuddin Hossain
judgment_text: Prompt dower becomes payable upon demand. So long as there is no formal demand by the wife and refusal by the husband, limitation under Article 103 does not begin to run during the subsistence of the conjugal relationship.
ratio_summary:
Prompt dower is payable immediately upon demand. Limitation under Article 103 of the Limitation Act runs only from the date when prompt dower is demanded and refused, or when marriage is dissolved. Non-demand during marriage creates no limitation bar.

[Controlling Statutes: The Family Courts Act, 2023 (4, 5), The Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, 1961 (10), The Limitation Act, 1908 (Article 103, Article 104)]

case_title: Unimarine S.A. vs Bangladesh Bank and others
judgment_text: The grounds for refusal of recognition and execution of a foreign arbitral award under Section 46 of the Act of 2001 are exhaustive. The court cannot sit as an appellate court to review the merits of the arbitral tribunal's determination.
ratio_summary:
Foreign arbitral awards under the New York Convention must be enforced as a decree of the court under Section 45. Recognition can only be refused on the exhaustive grounds in Section 46, such as public policy violation or invalidity of arbitration agreement.

[Controlling Statutes: The Arbitration Act, 2001 (45, 46, 47)]

case_title: KAFCO vs Karnaphuli Fertilizer Company Limited and others
judgment_text: Section 7A of the Arbitration Act, 2001 confers specific power on the court to grant interim protective orders in international commercial arbitration, irrespective of whether the arbitral seat is located within or outside the territory of Bangladesh.
ratio_summary:
Following the 2004 amendment adding Section 7A to the Arbitration Act 2001, civil courts in Bangladesh have statutory jurisdiction to grant interim measures of protection even if the place of arbitration is outside Bangladesh.

[Controlling Statutes: The Arbitration Act, 2001 (3, 7A, 45)]

case_title: Bangladesh Legal Aid and Services Trust (BLAST) and others vs Bangladesh and others
judgment_text: Section 54 of the Code of Criminal Procedure does not give arbitrary or unbridled power to a police officer to arrest anyone on simple suspicion. The Magistrate must strictly follow guidelines before granting detention in police custody under Section 167.
ratio_summary:
Arrest under Section 54 CrPC requires credible information and reasonable suspicion, not arbitrary whim. Police must disclose identity, inform relatives within 3 hours, and magistrates cannot grant police remand mechanically without hearing the accused and recording cogent legal grounds.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (54, 167, 176), The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 31, Article 32, Article 33)]

case_title: Syed Farhad Hossain vs State and another
judgment_text: To fasten vicarious liability under Section 141 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, there must be a specific assertion in the petition of complaint as to how and in what manner the concerned director was responsible for the conduct of the business of the company.
ratio_summary:
Under Section 141 of NI Act, vicarious criminal liability requires clear and specific averment in the complaint showing that the director was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business at the time the offence was committed.

[Controlling Statutes: The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (138, 141)]

case_title: Md. Humayun Kabir vs State and another
judgment_text: No cause of action arises to file a petition of complaint under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act before the expiry of 15 days from the date of receipt of the legal notice. Premature filing renders the proceeding void ab initio.
ratio_summary:
The statutory sequence under Section 138 of the NI Act is mandatory. Cause of action arises only after the drawer fails to make payment within 15 days of receiving the legal notice. A complaint filed before expiration of this 15-day period is premature and must be quashed.

[Controlling Statutes: The Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (138, 141)]

case_title: Secretary, Ministry of Finance vs Md. Masdar Hossain and others
judgment_text: The separation of the judiciary from the executive organs of the State is the basic feature of the Constitution. The judicial service is distinct and separate from civil executive services and must be administered independently under the superintendence of the Supreme Court.
ratio_summary:
Separation of the judiciary from the executive organs of the State is a basic pillar and constitutional mandate under Article 22. Subordinate courts must be under the exclusive administrative control and superintendence of the Supreme Court under Article 116.

[Controlling Statutes: The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 22, Article 109, Article 115, Article 116)]

case_title: Md. Jahangir Alam vs Anti-Corruption Commission (ACC) and another
judgment_text: Under Section 27(1) of the Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004, when the prosecution proves that the assets are disproportionate to known sources of income, the burden shifts to the accused to satisfactorily account for how the wealth was acquired.
ratio_summary:
Once the prosecution establishes that a public servant is in possession of pecuniary resources or property disproportionate to their known sources of lawful income, the statutory burden shifts to the accused under Section 27(1) to satisfactorily account for the same.

[Controlling Statutes: The Anti-Corruption Commission Act, 2004 (26, 27), The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (5)]

case_title: Robi Axiata Limited vs Commissioner of Large Taxpayers Unit (LTU-VAT)
judgment_text: In a taxing statute, one has to look merely at what is clearly said. There is no room for any intendment. Subjecting SIM replacement to tax without an explicit legislative charge is impermissible.
ratio_summary:
Taxing statutes must be construed strictly. In the absence of express statutory charging language taxing replacement of defective SIMs, administrative circulars cannot create a tax liability beyond the four corners of the Act.

[Controlling Statutes: The Value Added Tax Act, 1991 (3, 5, 55)]

case_title: Shamsun Nahar vs Principal, Holy Cross College and others
judgment_text: Educational authorities must exercise discretion fairly and transparently. Denying a student the right to sit in public examinations without granting an opportunity of being heard violates Article 27 and 31 of the Constitution.
ratio_summary:
Access to education and participation in public board examinations are fundamental aspects of protection under law. Educational institutions cannot act arbitrarily without conforming to the principles of natural justice and fair notice.

[Controlling Statutes: The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 27, Article 28, Article 31)]

case_title: Anowara Begum vs Md. Nurul Islam and others
judgment_text: Under Mahomedan Law, three conditions are necessary for a valid gift (Hiba): declaration of the gift by the donor, acceptance of the gift by the donee, and delivery of possession of the subject matter. Without delivery of possession, the gift is invalid.
ratio_summary:
For gifts executed prior to the 2004 statutory registration amendment, three essential elements must be proven to constitute a valid Muslim Hiba: (1) declaration of gift by donor, (2) acceptance by donee, and (3) complete delivery of actual or constructive possession.

[Controlling Statutes: The Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (122, 123, 129), The Registration Act, 1908 (17)]

case_title: Grameenphone Ltd vs Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission (BTRC)
judgment_text: When staying a statutory regulatory demand involving public revenue under Order 39 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court must balance the balance of convenience with public interest by directing a reasonable interim deposit.
ratio_summary:
In substantial revenue and regulatory audit disputes, the grant of an interlocutory injunction staying public revenue demands must be balanced with the public interest by requiring an equitable deposit.

[Controlling Statutes: The Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulation Act, 2001 (27, 30, 50), The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order 39 Rule 1)]

case_title: Government of Bangladesh vs Advocate Asaduzzaman Siddiqui and others
judgment_text: Independence of the judiciary is a fundamental pillar of the Constitution. Subjecting superior court judges to parliamentary removal impairs judicial independence and violates the basic structure of our constitutional framework.
ratio_summary:
Judicial independence is part of the inviolable basic structure of the Constitution. Empowering Parliament to remove judges on grounds of misconduct breaches separation of powers; the Supreme Judicial Council mechanism under Article 96 is essential for safeguarding judicial tenure.

[Controlling Statutes: The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 7, Article 22, Article 96, Article 116)]

case_title: Khandaker Delwar Hossain vs Bangladesh Italian Marble Works Ltd
judgment_text: The Constitution of Bangladesh is the supreme law and nobody is above it. Taking over power by extra-constitutional means and suspending the Constitution is treason and void ab initio.
ratio_summary:
The Constitution is the supreme law of the Republic under Article 7. Extra-constitutional takeover and martial law proclamations are ultra vires, void ab initio, and cannot be validated by subsequent constitutional amendments.

[Controlling Statutes: The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 7, Article 26, Article 142)]

judgment_text: Where a person has knowledge of structural cracks and continues to force workers into the building, the element of knowledge under Section 304 Part II of the Penal Code is attracted, taking it out of the purview of simple negligence.
ratio_summary:
Operating unauthorized heavy commercial machinery in a visibly fractured building with knowledge that it is likely to cause death falls within Section 304 (culpable homicide not amounting to murder) rather than mere rash and negligent act under Section 304A.

[Controlling Statutes: The Penal Code, 1860 (304, 304A, 337), The Building Construction Act, 1952 (3, 12)]

case_title: Al-Arafah Islami Bank Ltd vs M/S R.R. Trading and others
judgment_text: Upon issuance of a certificate under Section 33(7) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003, the right, title, and interest in the mortgaged property vest completely in the decree-holder financial institution.
ratio_summary:
When mortgaged property remains unsold after successive auctions in execution, a certificate issued under Section 33(7) of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 vests absolute title in the decree-holder bank, entitling it to seek immediate delivery of possession through court.

[Controlling Statutes: The Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 (33, 34)]

case_title: Rashida Khatun vs Md. Kamal Hossain
judgment_text: To constitute dowry under the Act, property or valuable security must be demanded as consideration for the marriage. Customary gifts voluntarily presented without demand cannot form the basis of a criminal prosecution.
ratio_summary:
Dowry demands require a coercive condition for marriage or continuation of marital life. Voluntary traditional gifts given without demand or coercion do not fall within the penal definition of dowry under the Act.

[Controlling Statutes: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 2018 (2, 3, 4), The Penal Code, 1860 (498A)]

case_title: Nurul Islam vs Bangladesh and others
judgment_text: In an appeal against acquittal under Section 417 of the Code, the appellate court must exercise caution. If the view taken by the trial judge is a reasonably plausible view on the evidence, the acquittal cannot be reversed.
ratio_summary:
An order of acquittal strengthens the initial presumption of innocence. An appellate court should not interfere with an acquittal merely because an alternative view is possible; interference requires perverse or illegal findings by the trial court.

[Controlling Statutes: The Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898 (417, 423), The Evidence Act, 1872 (3, 101)]

case_title: Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers Association (BELA) vs Ministry of Environment
judgment_text: Protection of the environment under Article 18A is a constitutional obligation. The Precautionary Principle and Polluter Pays Principle form part of the environmental jurisprudence of Bangladesh.
ratio_summary:
Article 18A of the Constitution imposes an affirmative constitutional duty on the State to protect the environment. No commercial entity can operate in an ecologically critical zone without a valid Environmental Clearance Certificate.

[Controlling Statutes: The Bangladesh Environment Conservation Act, 1995 (6A, 12), The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 18A, Article 32)]

case_title: Dr. Shirin Akhtar vs Ministry of Land and others
judgment_text: The State cannot dispossess a citizen of private property under the colour of acquisition without strictly complying with the statutory requirement of prior assessment and payment of compensation.
ratio_summary:
Under property acquisition laws and Article 42 of the Constitution, statutory compensation must be determined and disbursed before taking possession of private land for public purpose.

[Controlling Statutes: Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act, 2017 (4, 7, 8), The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 42)]

judgment_text: When a question involves the constitutional validity of a treaty ceding territory of the Republic, any citizen has a sufficient interest to maintain a petition under Article 102 of the Constitution.
ratio_summary:
Where a constitutional question of grave public importance arises affecting the territory or governance of the Republic, any citizen has locus standi to invoke the writ jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102.

[Controlling Statutes: The Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh (Article 102, Article 143)]
